# Exercise 1.1 — Python vs R {#sec-python-r}

::::: web-only
## The libraries

A note on vocabulary. R calls them **packages** and loads them with `library(dplyr)`; Python calls them **modules** or **packages** and loads them with `import pandas as pd` or `from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score`. Then in R, `library(dplyr)` puts *every* dplyr function within reach, whereas Python makes you name what you want. That is why R code reads `filter(...)` and Python code reads `pd.read_csv(...)` — the prefix tells you where the function came from, and in R you have to remember.

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

### Key R packages

#### The tidyverse — getting data into shape

[tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/) is not one package but a family that shares a design: data frames in, data frames out, verbs that read as English (for example, a dplyr pipeline is a *sentence*. `data |> filter(age > 60) |> summarise(mean(los))` reads left to right in the order the work happens) and the pipe (`|>` or `%>%`) to chain them. `library(tidyverse)` loads them all at once. The key packages `tidyverse`contains are:

| Package | What it does |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| [readr](https://readr.tidyverse.org/) | reads `.csv` into a data frame — `read_csv()` |
| [dplyr](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/) | the verbs: `filter`, `select`, `mutate`, `group_by`, `summarise`, `arrange` |
| [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) | plots built by adding layers — `ggplot() + geom_point()` |
| [tidyr](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/) | reshaping between wide and long — `pivot_longer()` |

### tidymodels — fitting and evaluating

[tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org/) is also a collection of packages.It is to modelling what the tidyverse is to data handling: a family of packages with one grammar. Its central idea is that *specifying* a model is separate from *fitting* it, and separate again from *which implementation* does the arithmetic. Key packages it contains are:

| Package | What it does |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| [parsnip](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/) | one vocabulary for many models — `linear_reg()`, `logistic_reg()`, `rand_forest()` |
| [recipes](https://recipes.tidymodels.org/) | preprocessing as a fitted object — `step_normalize()`, `step_impute_mean()` |
| [rsample](https://rsample.tidymodels.org/) | splitting and resampling — `initial_split()`, `vfold_cv()` |
| [yardstick](https://yardstick.tidymodels.org/) | evaluation metrics — `rmse()`, `roc_auc()`, `sens()`, `spec()` |

**To call a specific ML algorithm you set an engine.** For example, `set_engine("ranger")` means "fit this random forest using the ranger package". The specification stays the same; the engine is swapped.

| Engine | Package | Used for |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| `"lm"`, `"glm"` | base R | linear and logistic regression |
| `"rpart"` | [rpart](https://cran.r-project.org/package=rpart) | a single decision tree |
| `"ranger"` | [ranger](https://imbs-hl.github.io/ranger/) | random forests, fast |
| `"glmnet"` | [glmnet](https://glmnet.stanford.edu/) | lasso and ridge |

### Key Python packages

### The scientific stack

| Library | What it does |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/) | the `DataFrame` — `read_csv()`, `groupby()`, `describe()` |
| [numpy](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/) | arrays and the maths on them; what pandas is built on |
| [matplotlib](https://matplotlib.org/stable/) | plots, built by commanding an `Axes` object |
| [scipy](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/) | scientific algorithms; here `optimize.minimize` |

### scikit-learn

In [scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) every object follows the same contract: `.fit(X, y)` learns from data, `.transform(X)` or `.predict(X)` applies what was learned, and `.fit_transform()` does both. Once you know that, a model you have never seen before is usable in one line.

It is organised into submodules and here are a few to note:

| Submodule | What lives there |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `linear_model` | `LinearRegression`, `LogisticRegression`, `Lasso` |
| `model_selection` | `train_test_split`, `cross_val_score`, `GridSearchCV` |
| `metrics` | `mean_absolute_error`, `roc_auc_score`, `confusion_matrix` |
| `preprocessing` | `StandardScaler`, `MinMaxScaler`, `OneHotEncoder` |
| `pipeline` | `Pipeline` — the object that makes leakage hard to commit |
| `compose` | `ColumnTransformer` — different preprocessing per column |
| `impute` | `SimpleImputer`, `IterativeImputer` |
| `tree`, `ensemble` | `DecisionTreeClassifier`, `RandomForestClassifier` |
| `inspection` | `permutation_importance`, `partial_dependence` |
| `dummy` | `DummyClassifier` — the baseline you must beat |

The [scikit-learn user guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html) explains the statistics as well as the code, and is worth reading.

## The same job in both languages

| Job | R | Python |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| read a csv | `readr::read_csv()` | `pandas.read_csv()` |
| filter rows | `dplyr::filter()` | `df[df.col > x]` or `df.query()` |
| group and summarise | `dplyr::group_by() \|> summarise()` | `df.groupby().agg()` |
| plot | `ggplot2` | `matplotlib` |
| split train/test | `rsample::initial_split()` | `train_test_split()` |
| preprocess without leaking | `recipes` inside a `workflow()` | `Pipeline` + `ColumnTransformer` |
| fit a model | `parsnip` spec `\|> fit()` | `estimator.fit(X, y)` |
| score it | `yardstick` | `sklearn.metrics` |

## If a library is missing

A missing package produces `Error in library(x) : there is no package called 'x'` in R, or `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'x'` in Python. Install it:

``` r
install.packages("naniar")
```

``` python
pip install shap
```

Every cell on this page is a real R or Python cell. Copy the code in your chosen language, run it, and read the output. Then read the other tab. Python code will appear as **vermillion** and R as **blue**.
:::::

## Lets see them in action

Lets create a dataset of five patients with two columns: `age` in years, and `score`, an Injury Severity Score.

::: panel-tabset
## R

```{r}
data <- data.frame(
  age   = c(23, 45, 12, 56, 70),
  score = c(87, 56, 30, 77, 80)
)
data
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd

data = pd.DataFrame({
    "age":   [23, 45, 12, 56, 70],
    "score": [87, 56, 30, 77, 80]
})
data
```
:::

## Data wrangling: `pandas` → `dplyr`, from the tidyverse

Both are for data wrangling: selecting, filtering, sorting, summarising. Here, keeping only the patients over 20.

::: panel-tabset
## R

```{r}
#| message: false
library(dplyr)

filtered_data <- data %>% filter(age > 20)
head(filtered_data)
```

## Python

```{python}
filtered_data = data[data["age"] > 20]
filtered_data.head()
```
:::

## ML pipeline: `scikit-learn` → `tidymodels`

Both are for building machine learning pipelines. Here, fitting a linear regression of score on age.

In R you have already done this in Module 2, with `lm()` from the `stats` package in base R:

```{r}
model <- lm(score ~ age, data = data)
summary(model)
```

In Python the same fit comes from scikit-learn:

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model_py = LinearRegression()
X = data[["age"]]    # 2-D: a frame, because sklearn expects a matrix of predictors
y = data["score"]    # 1-D: a series, the target

model_py.fit(X, y)
print(model_py.intercept_, model_py.coef_)
```

The coefficients agree!

What differs is what each returns. `lm()` hands back a statistical summary — standard errors, residuals, an F test — because R's linear model was written for inference. `LinearRegression` hands back coefficients and a `.predict()` method, because scikit-learn's was written for prediction.

R can also do it the scikit-learn/ML way. `tidymodels` sets the model up in the same three moves — define the algorithm, give it the data, fit it:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| 
library(tidymodels)

lm_model <- linear_reg() %>%
            set_engine("lm") %>%      # use lm()'s implementation underneath
            set_mode("regression")

lm_fit <- lm_model %>%
          fit(score ~ age, data = data)

lm_fit[["fit"]][["coefficients"]]
```

Note what `set_engine("lm")` is doing: the specification above says *linear regression* and nothing about how to compute it, and the engine supplies the arithmetic. Swap in `"glmnet"` and the first half of that code is unchanged.

## Visualization: `matplotlib, seaborn` → `ggplot2`

Both are for plotting. Here, a scatter of score against age.

::: panel-tabset
## R

```{r}
#| message: false
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = score)) +
  geom_point()
```

## Python

```{python}
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sns.scatterplot(x = data["age"], y = data["score"])
plt.show()
```
:::

The `+` in ggplot2 is not decoration. A plot is a stack of layers and you add them one at a time, which is why the next task is a one-line change rather than a rewrite.

## Algebra:`numpy` → base R

numpy is Python's array library; in R, arrays and the arithmetic on them are in the language itself (preloaded package called `base`) , so there is nothing to load. Here, a dot product.

::: panel-tabset
## R

```{r}
a <- c(1, 2, 3)
b <- c(4, 5, 6)
dot_product <- sum(a * b)
dot_product
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([4, 5, 6])
dot_product = np.dot(a, b)
print(dot_product)
```
:::

`a * b` multiplies element by element in both languages, and `sum()` adds the result. `np.dot` does both in one step.

For actual matrix work R has the operators built in: `%*%` is matrix multiplication and `solve()` is the inverse --- though `solve(A, b)` solves `Ax = b` without ever forming that inverse, which is what you normally want. So `a %*% b` is the dot product too, but watch the type: it returns a 1x1 *matrix* rather than a single number, and that difference will eventually bite you inside an `if`. `sum(a * b)` returns a plain number. The Python equivalents are `A @ B` and `np.linalg.solve`.

## Exercise: Put the regression on the plot

Add the fitted line to the scatter. In ggplot2 it is one more layer: look up `geom_smooth()` and give it `method = "lm"`. Then find the Python equivalent — seaborn has a function that draws a scatter *and* its regression line together.

::::::: panel-tabset
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = score)) +
  geom_point() +
  ______(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

:::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer

```{r}
#| message: false
ggplot(data, aes(x = age, y = score)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

`se = FALSE` turns off the confidence band. Leave it on and you will see how wide it is with five points, which is an honest picture of what this data can support.
:::
::::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
sns.______(x = "age", y = "score", data = data)
plt.show()
```

:::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer

```{python}
sns.regplot(x = "age", y = "score", data = data)
plt.show()
```

`sns.regplot()` draws the points and fits the line in one call. `sns.lmplot()` does the same and will also split the plot by a grouping column.
:::
::::
:::::::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?

In R the layer you want starts with `geom_`. In Python the seaborn function you want starts with `reg`.
:::
